title: Bamidbar: banners around the center (Numbers 2)
hookLine: each tribe camps under its own banner, all facing the sanctuary

cards: A wedding seating chart is a small war. The bride's cousins at one table, the groom's college friends at another, two great-aunts who must never sit together.

Every table different, every table set around the same dance floor. Now take away the hall, put it in the desert, and make it twelve tribes, hundreds of thousands of people, setting up camp every time they stop.
You'd expect a scramble. Numbers chapter two draws a map instead, and the shape of that map is the lesson.

teach.h: DEGEL: EACH BY HIS OWN BANNER.
teach.b: The instruction is simple. The children of Israel will camp each one by his own banner, with the signs of their fathers' houses, around the tent of meeting, at a distance. The Hebrew word for banner is degel.
Twelve tribes form four camps of three. To the east, toward the sunrise, Judah leads, with Issachar and Zebulun. To the south, Reuben.
To the west, Ephraim. To the north, Dan. Inside that ring, the Levites camp in a closer circle, and at the very center stands the Tabernacle.
When they march, they march in that order, and when they stop, the same square forms again. The map does two things at once. First, everyone keeps their own banner.
No tribe is told to blend in. Rashi, following the midrash, says each banner had its own color, matching that tribe's stone on the high priest's breastplate.
Second, every banner is set around the same middle: they camp round about the tent of meeting, on every side of it.
The differences are real, and they're arranged around something shared. A later midrash imagines the nations of the world looking at this camp with longing, not for its size, but for its order.
It's an old picture of a people that is many and one at the same time. You don't have to stop being your tribe to be part of the whole. You just have to face the center.

how: The arrangement of the camp in Numbers 2 is read in the portion Bamidbar; some synagogues display the twelve tribal symbols, and teachers use the camp as a picture of a people that keeps its many identities around one shared center.

games.why: four camps of three, each with its own banner, and the Tabernacle at the center. many, facing one middle.

practice: Ask what your banner is, your family, your town, your background, your way of praying or not praying, and be glad of it for a moment.
Then picture someone you live or work beside who flies a different one, and be glad of theirs, too. Last, ask what center you share with them: a street, a project, a child, a table.
